title: Adaptive haptic feedback cuts grasp failures by 31% at 500 ms
background: Remote operators lose grasp precision once the round-trip delay goes above about 200 ms.
Can touch (haptic) feedback that adapts to the delay keep remote grasps reliable?
analysis: Each of 24 participants made remote grasps at 50, 250 and 500 ms of delay, with adaptive and with fixed haptic gain (feedback strength).
NASA resources used: [name them, or none]

callout.label: fewer grasp failures with adaptive haptic feedback
callout.context: than with fixed haptic gain at 500 ms of delay, 24 participants

figures.alt: Callout: 31% fewer grasp failures with latency-adaptive haptic feedback than with fixed haptic gain at 500 ms of delay, 24 participants.

caption: Fig. 1: fewer grasp failures (%) at 500 ms, n = 24
significance: At 500 ms of delay, adaptive feedback cut grasp failures by 31% compared with fixed feedback.
Robots operated over slow links, such as lunar surface robots driven from Earth, could grasp reliably without waiting for faster networks.
notes: Methods: within-subjects study. Each of 24 participants performed remote grasps in three latency conditions (50, 250 and 500 ms), with latency-adaptive haptic gain and with fixed haptic gain. [Add the task, apparatus and statistical test from the paper.]

Result: at 500 ms, adaptive feedback cut grasp failures by 31% compared with fixed feedback. The paper reports this value only, so the Results panel states it as a callout; [add the 50 ms and 250 ms results from the paper if a comparison chart is wanted].

Acronyms: RA-L = IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters; EPSCoR = Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research; ms = milliseconds; haptic gain = the strength of the force feedback the operator feels.
